calc_items.title: Mid-parental target height (boy)
calc_items.question: A boy's mother is 158 cm and his father 174 cm tall. Calculate his mid-parental target height = (mother + father + 13)/2.

calc_items.title: Mid-parental target height (girl)
calc_items.question: A girl's mother is 160 cm and her father 174 cm tall. Calculate her mid-parental target height = (mother + father − 13)/2.

calc_items.title: Height velocity (12 months)
calc_items.question: Height rises from 110 cm to 115 cm over 12 months. Calculate the annualised height velocity.

calc_items.title: Height velocity (6 months)
calc_items.question: Height rises from 120 cm to 123 cm over 6 months. Calculate the annualised height velocity.

calc_items.title: Height velocity (9 months)
calc_items.question: Height rises from 102 cm to 105 cm over 9 months. Calculate the annualised height velocity.

1.A: GH is secreted in pulses, so a random level is usually low even in normal children and cannot separate variant from pathology; auxology must come first.
1.C: A single weight percentile says nothing about the linear growth pattern; serial height and growth velocity define whether growth is failing.
1.D: A single cortisol is not a screen for short stature and is only relevant when a specific adrenal or Cushing picture is suspected.

2.B: Turner syndrome shows progressive growth decline with falling velocity and no family history of late puberty; karyotype is reserved when the pattern is not reassuring.
2.C: Acquired hypothyroidism causes markedly reduced growth velocity with weight gain, not normal velocity with a familial late-maturation pattern.
2.D: Skeletal dysplasia causes disproportionate short stature, not proportionate growth with delayed bone age and familial late puberty.

3.A: Untreated coeliac disease causes poor weight gain, slowed growth velocity and delayed bone age, unlike this normal-velocity, normal-bone-age child of short parents.
3.B: GH deficiency causes subnormal growth velocity and delayed bone age, whereas here both are normal.
3.D: Cushing syndrome causes growth arrest with weight gain, not normal growth velocity in a child of short parents.

4.A: Trisomy 21 is almost always clinically obvious from dysmorphism and developmental delay, so it is not the hidden cause in a non-dysmorphic short girl.
4.C: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) occurs in males and is associated with tall rather than short stature.
4.D: Fragile X mainly presents with intellectual disability and behavioural features, not isolated short stature in girls.

5.B: Total T3 alone is often maintained until late hypothyroidism and is affected by binding proteins, so it misses most hypothyroid children.
5.C: Thyroglobulin is not a test of thyroid function; it is used in dysgenesis work-up and thyroid cancer follow-up.
5.D: Random GH is pulsatile and non-diagnostic, and constipation with fatigue points to the thyroid axis first.

6.A: Low height with low weight-for-height suggests undernutrition or systemic disease, where weight falls before or with height.
6.C: Chronic diarrhoea with wasting points to a gastrointestinal or malabsorptive cause such as coeliac disease, not an endocrine one.
6.D: Severe undernutrition reduces weight more than height and is a systemic, not endocrine, cause of growth failure.

7.A: Recalled heights are unreliable and cannot substitute for an accurate standardised measurement.
7.B: Supine length is used under 2 years; a 10-year-old should be measured standing on a stadiometer.
7.D: Arm span is a proportion check or a height surrogate only when standing height cannot be measured, not a correction for poor technique.

8.A: GH stimulation does not address disproportion or bowing; skeletal dysplasia or rickets must be assessed first.
8.B: Thyroid antibodies do not explain disproportionate stature with bowed legs and would miss rickets or dysplasia.
8.C: Constitutional delay produces proportionate short stature without limb deformity, so excluding it is not the priority here.

9.B: A height on the 25th percentile with a stable trajectory is normal growth and needs no investigation.
9.C: A single inconsistent measurement should be repeated, not investigated, as it may be measurement error.
9.D: Tall parents alone are not a finding needing work-up, though they make a falling trajectory more concerning in context.

10.A: GH is not secreted continuously; its pulsatile release is exactly why random levels mislead.
10.C: GH is measured in serum; urinary GH is not a standard diagnostic test.
10.D: GH drives hepatic IGF-1 production, which is why IGF-1 is used as a screening marker.

11.A: Malnutrition itself lowers IGF-1, so a low value cannot define isolated GH deficiency without stimulation testing and auxology.
11.B: Acromegaly or GH excess raises IGF-1, the opposite of this finding.
11.D: A low IGF-1 is non-specific and is not evidence of a pituitary tumour, which needs imaging and endocrine assessment.

12.B: Familial tall stature is the opposite of severe growth failure and lacks hypoglycaemia or micropenis.
12.C: Iron deficiency does not cause neonatal hypoglycaemia or micropenis.
12.D: Simple obesity is associated with normal or accelerated linear growth, not severe growth failure with hypopituitary clues.

13.A: Low height alone does not establish GH deficiency; other causes and pituitary axes must be evaluated before treatment.
13.C: Bone age is part of the standard evaluation and helps assess growth potential, so it should not be avoided.
13.D: Random GH is pulsatile and cannot be a diagnostic criterion.

14.A: Appendicitis does not explain headache with visual symptoms and is not a GH-related adverse effect.
14.B: Iron deficiency does not produce headache, vomiting and visual disturbance as a GH complication.
14.D: Rhinitis does not cause vomiting and visual symptoms; attributing these to a viral illness risks missing raised intracranial pressure.

15.A: Otitis media does not cause limp or hip pain.
15.C: Nephrotic syndrome presents with oedema and proteinuria, not hip pain, and is not a GH complication.
15.D: Lactose intolerance causes gastrointestinal symptoms, not limp or hip pain.

16.A: A single test has a high false-positive rate; usually two different stimuli are needed for diagnosis.
16.B: Results vary with pubertal status (hence sex-steroid priming) and with the assay used.
16.C: Testing is needed in many children with suspected GH deficiency, though not every GH-treated condition requires it.

17.B: Central hypothyroidism has low free T4 with low or inappropriately normal TSH, not a high TSH.
17.C: A euthyroid state has normal TSH and free T4.
17.D: Thyrotoxicosis has suppressed TSH with high thyroid hormones.

18.A: Graves disease gives suppressed TSH with high free T4.
18.C: Iodine excess typically causes primary hypothyroidism with raised TSH, not low free T4 with normal TSH.
18.D: Subclinical hyperthyroidism has low TSH with normal free T4.

19.A: Ferritin is unrelated to the risk of starting thyroxine in hypopituitarism.
19.B: Calcium does not address the key danger of precipitating adrenal crisis.
19.D: Urinary catecholamines screen for phaeochromocytoma or neuroblastoma, not pituitary-adrenal insufficiency.

20.A: Delaying to 6 months risks irreversible neurodevelopmental damage; treatment should start within the first weeks of life.
20.B: School age is far too late; the brain-critical window is infancy.
20.C: Most affected newborns are asymptomatic; waiting for symptoms defeats the purpose of screening.

21.B: Congenital GH deficiency does not cause goitre, anti-TPO antibodies or raised TSH.
21.C: Central diabetes insipidus causes polyuria and polydipsia and has no link to goitre or TPO antibodies.
21.D: Hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcaemia, not goitre with raised TSH and anti-TPO positivity.

22.A: Primary hypothyroidism has high TSH and low free T4 with bradycardia and weight gain.
22.C: GH deficiency does not cause tachycardia, tremor or abnormal thyroid tests.
22.D: Central hypothyroidism has low free T4, not high, and causes hypometabolic features.

23.A: Anti-dsDNA is a marker of systemic lupus erythematosus.
23.B: Anti-mitochondrial antibody is a marker of primary biliary cholangitis.
23.D: Anti-CCP is a marker of rheumatoid arthritis.

24.A: Mild hunger reflects thyrotoxicosis or its recovery and is not a drug toxicity warning.
24.B: Improved sleep indicates clinical improvement, not an adverse effect.
24.C: A growth spurt is not a recognised toxicity of antithyroid drugs.

25.A: Overt hypothyroidism requires a low free T4, which is normal here.
25.C: Central hyperthyroidism (TSH-secreting adenoma) has high free T4 with non-suppressed TSH, not a normal free T4.
25.D: Thyroid storm is a severe thyrotoxic crisis with suppressed TSH and high thyroid hormones.

26.B: Familial short stature shows normal height velocity parallel to the centiles within the parental target; a falling height velocity is not expected.
26.C: Constitutional delay shows normal prepubertal height velocity with delayed bone age and a family history of late puberty, not progressive velocity decline with relative weight gain.
26.D: Nutritional deprivation lowers weight before height, giving a low BMI; the preserved-to-high BMI here points to an endocrine cause.

27.A: Spot cortisol assesses adrenal function and gives no information about body proportions or skeletal disproportion.
27.C: Random GH is pulsatile and uninformative, and GH deficiency causes proportionate short stature, so it does not characterize disproportion.
27.D: Serum ferritin reflects iron stores; it is irrelevant to measuring limb-versus-trunk proportions.

28.A: Subtracting 13 cm is the correction used for girls, which would underestimate a boy's target height.
28.B: This is not an averaging formula; subtracting maternal from paternal height gives no meaningful target height.
28.C: A simple parental mean ignores the average 13 cm adult sex difference, so it underestimates target height for a boy.

29.B: 167 cm is the simple parental mean without the 13 cm female correction.
29.C: 173.5 cm is obtained by adding 13 cm, the formula for boys, not girls.
29.D: 154 cm does not correspond to any standard midparental calculation; (160 + 174 − 13)/2 gives 160.5 cm.

30.B: A single height with weight gives a point-in-time status, not a rate of growth over time.
30.C: Bone age estimates skeletal maturity and growth potential but cannot measure how fast the child is growing.
30.D: A random GH level is pulsatile and says nothing about the rate of linear growth.

31.A: Disproportionate limb shortening suggests skeletal dysplasia, not nutritional growth failure.
31.C: Height faltering with preserved weight gain is the endocrine pattern (e.g. GH deficiency, hypothyroidism, glucocorticoid excess).
31.D: Undernutrition slows rather than accelerates linear growth.

32.A: Urinary catecholamines screen for neuroblastoma or phaeochromocytoma, which do not explain cubitus valgus and recurrent otitis.
32.B: Sweat chloride tests for cystic fibrosis, which causes growth failure through malabsorption but not cubitus valgus.
32.D: Serum ammonia evaluates urea cycle or liver disorders and has no role in this Turner-like phenotype.

33.A: Adult BMI cut-offs are not valid in young children, whose BMI varies with age.
33.B: Tanner adult centiles are not used for term infants aged 0–5 years in WHO-based practice.
33.C: Bone-age tables assess skeletal maturity and are not growth charts for monitoring infants.

34.A: Using uncorrected age makes a preterm infant appear smaller, so it underestimates rather than overestimates the percentile.
34.C: Lack of correction distorts the percentile but does not cause all endocrine disease to be missed.
34.D: Bone age is read from radiographs and is not affected by how weight or length is plotted.

35.A: Simple obesity does not cause short length or body disproportion; obese children are usually tall for age.
35.C: Constitutional delay produces proportionate short stature, not marked disproportion in infancy.
35.D: Graves disease is rare in infancy and accelerates growth; it does not cause disproportionate short length.

36.A: Lumbar spine imaging may help in skeletal dysplasia but does not identify the cause of GH deficiency.
36.B: Abdominal aorta imaging has no role in evaluating the GH axis.
36.D: Temporal lobe imaging alone misses the sella, pituitary stalk and hypothalamus, where relevant anomalies lie.

37.A: Vitamin D excess is not a feature of hypopituitarism and does not explain hypoglycaemia.
37.B: Primary hyperparathyroidism is a parathyroid disorder unrelated to midline defects or pituitary deficiency.
37.C: Calcitonin excess suggests medullary thyroid carcinoma, not combined pituitary hormone deficiency.

38.B: Hypothyroidism blunts rather than raises GH secretion, so falsely high GH is not the concern.
38.C: Hypothyroidism does not cause pituitary calcification; long-standing primary hypothyroidism may cause pituitary hyperplasia instead.
38.D: Hypothyroidism does not affect the accuracy of stadiometry; the issue is a falsely low GH response.

39.A: Growth chart trajectory with serial measurements is a cornerstone of screening for GH deficiency.
39.C: Reduced height velocity is a key clinical criterion that prompts GH axis evaluation.
39.D: Age- and puberty-referenced IGF-1 is a useful integrated screen of GH status, though not definitive.

40.A: Thyroidectomy is an inappropriate intervention; nothing suggests thyroid disease requiring surgery.
40.B: Pituitary surgery has no role without a demonstrated pituitary lesion, and the features point to malabsorption.
40.D: Starting GH without investigation would miss a treatable cause such as coeliac disease.

41.A: Low IGF-1 alone cannot prove GH deficiency, especially when undernutrition may lower it.
41.B: Acromegaly causes high, not low, IGF-1.
41.C: A low IGF-1 does not rule out chronic disease; chronic illness and malnutrition commonly lower it.

42.B: Appendicitis causes abdominal pain and fever; visual symptoms with headache suggest raised intracranial pressure.
42.C: Hyperparathyroidism is not a recognised complication of GH therapy and does not cause visual symptoms.
42.D: Iron overload is unrelated to GH therapy and does not present with acute headache and visual disturbance.

43.A: Scoliosis progression can occur on GH but causes back deformity, not limp with hip pain.
43.C: Clubfoot is a congenital foot deformity, not an acquired complication of GH therapy.
43.D: Osgood–Schlatter causes tibial tubercle (knee) pain; hip pain with limp on GH requires exclusion of SCFE.

44.A: Glucocorticoids do not cause GH excess, and the stem describes growth failure rather than accelerated maturation.
44.B: Chronic glucocorticoid exposure does not cause thyrotoxicosis; if anything it suppresses TSH.
44.D: Glucocorticoids reduce, not increase, growth velocity.

45.A: GH deficiency causes short stature and slow growth, the opposite of this presentation.
45.B: Congenital hypothyroidism causes short stature and coarse features but not tall stature with rapid growth.
45.C: Familial short stature is a normal variant with short height, not tall stature or coarse features.

46.B: Random insulin does not assess GH secretion and is not a screen for GH excess.
46.C: Urine glucose may reflect secondary diabetes but is neither sensitive nor specific for GH excess.
46.D: Serum calcium is not a screening test for GH excess.

47.A: TSH-receptor antibodies are an adjunct for suspected maternal autoimmune transient hypothyroidism, not the primary confirmation.
47.C: Total T3 is often maintained in hypothyroidism and does not confirm the diagnosis; free T4 with TSH is needed.
47.D: Thyroglobulin helps classify aetiology (e.g. athyreosis) but does not confirm thyroid dysfunction.

48.A: Diabetes insipidus presents with polyuria, dehydration and hypernatraemia, not macroglossia or a large fontanelle.
48.B: Cushing syndrome is very rare in neonates and does not cause macroglossia or a large posterior fontanelle.
48.D: Neonatal Graves disease causes tachycardia, irritability and goitre, not prolonged jaundice with macroglossia.

49.A: Waiting for speech delay means irreversible neurodevelopmental damage has already occurred.
49.B: Iodine alone does not treat dysgenesis or dyshormonogenesis; levothyroxine is standard therapy.
49.C: Delaying treatment until age 2 years would cause permanent intellectual impairment; therapy should start within the first two weeks.

50.B: Primary hypothyroidism produces an elevated TSH; a non-elevated TSH with low FT4 argues against it.
50.C: Graves disease causes high FT4 with suppressed TSH, not low FT4.
50.D: Iodine excess can cause hypothyroidism, usually with raised TSH, and the word always makes this option incorrect.

51.A: Radioiodine is a definitive treatment for hyperthyroidism and has no role in a child about to start levothyroxine for central hypothyroidism.
51.C: Cortisol status must be assessed, not avoided; missed central adrenal insufficiency can be unmasked into adrenal crisis once levothyroxine accelerates cortisol clearance.
51.D: Methimazole blocks thyroid hormone synthesis and treats hyperthyroidism; it would worsen a child who needs thyroid replacement.

52.A: Normal TSH with high FT4 suggests assay interference, TSH-secreting adenoma or thyroid hormone resistance, not primary hypothyroidism.
52.B: Low TSH with normal FT4 indicates subclinical hyperthyroidism or non-thyroidal illness, the opposite direction of primary thyroid failure.
52.D: Suppressed TSH with high FT4 is the pattern of primary thyrotoxicosis, not hypothyroidism.

53.A: High TSH with low FT4 is the pattern of primary hypothyroidism, the opposite of thyrotoxicosis.
53.B: Low FT4 with an inappropriately normal TSH suggests central hypothyroidism, not thyroid hormone excess.
53.C: Raised TSH with normal FT4 defines subclinical hypothyroidism; in primary thyrotoxicosis TSH is suppressed.

54.B: Thyroid storm is an acute decompensated thyrotoxic state with fever and tachycardia, and TSH would be suppressed, not high.
54.C: A pituitary adenoma would cause low or inappropriately normal TSH with central hypothyroidism, or TSH-driven hyperthyroidism, and does not explain anti-TPO positivity.
54.D: A thyroglossal duct cyst is a midline neck swelling that moves on tongue protrusion; it does not cause diffuse goitre, raised TSH or anti-TPO antibodies.

55.A: Delayed relaxation of deep-tendon reflexes is a classical hypothyroid sign; Graves disease causes brisk reflexes.
55.C: Bradycardia reflects hypothyroidism; thyroid hormone excess in Graves disease causes tachycardia.
55.D: Constipation is typical of hypothyroidism; Graves disease more often causes increased stool frequency.

56.A: Fever and sore throat on methimazole suggest agranulocytosis; increasing the dose could worsen a potentially fatal marrow toxicity.
56.B: Iodine is only a short-term adjunct, and switching without review ignores the urgent need to exclude agranulocytosis with a blood count.
56.D: Reassurance without a CBC risks missing agranulocytosis, which can progress rapidly to life-threatening sepsis.

57.A: PTU is an effective antithyroid drug; it is avoided because of hepatotoxicity, not lack of efficacy.
57.B: PTU does not cause congenital hypothyroidism in all exposed infants; it is even preferred in the first trimester of pregnancy.
57.C: PTU inhibits thyroid peroxidase and peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion, so it clearly has antithyroid action.

58.B: Overt primary hypothyroidism requires a low FT4; here FT4 is normal and the TSH rise is mild.
58.C: Central hypothyroidism shows low FT4 with low or inappropriately normal TSH, not a raised TSH with normal FT4.
58.D: Thyroid storm is severe decompensated thyrotoxicosis with suppressed TSH; this child is asymptomatic with a mildly raised TSH.

59.A: Urinary ketones do not assess slowing growth or constipation and ignore the high risk of hypothyroidism in Down syndrome.
59.C: A random GH level is uninformative because GH is pulsatile, and thyroid dysfunction is the more likely and treatable cause here.
59.D: Serum copper is relevant to Wilson disease or copper deficiency, not to the hypothyroid-like picture common in Down syndrome.

60.A: No programme detects every case; TSH-based screens miss central hypothyroidism and delayed TSH rise can be missed in preterm or sick infants.
60.B: A normal newborn screen never overrides clinical suspicion; symptomatic infants still need serum TSH and FT4.
60.D: Many programmes, including most Indian ones, use primary TSH screening; FT4 or T4 is not measured universally.

61.A: Graves disease causes suppressed TSH and high FT4, the opposite of this profile.
61.B: GH excess does not raise TSH or lower FT4; the history of poor adherence explains the biochemistry.
61.C: High TSH with low FT4 is clearly abnormal and indicates under-replacement, not euthyroidism.

62.B: Levothyroxine is ideally taken with water alone, which does not impair absorption.
62.C: Fasting administration is the recommended way to maximise levothyroxine absorption.
62.D: Separating calcium by several hours is the correct strategy to avoid binding and preserve absorption.

63.A: Dermatoglyphics form in early fetal life and are not affected by postnatal thyroid treatment timing.
63.C: Eye colour is genetically determined and unrelated to thyroid hormone exposure.
63.D: ABO blood group is genetically fixed and unaffected by congenital hypothyroidism or its treatment.

64.A: Thyroid agenesis causes congenital hypothyroidism with no thyroid tissue, not thyrotoxicosis with a vascular goitre.
64.B: Central hypothyroidism causes low thyroid hormone, not thyrotoxicosis, and produces no goitre or orbitopathy.
64.D: Hashimoto thyroiditis may have a transient thyrotoxic phase but lacks orbitopathy and a vascular goitre with bruit, which point to Graves disease.

65.A: In central hypothyroidism TSH is low or inappropriately normal and does not reflect replacement adequacy, so it cannot guide titration.
65.B: Anti-TPO titre indicates autoimmune aetiology and plays no role in dosing for pituitary-stalk-related central hypothyroidism.
65.C: Thyroglobulin reflects thyroid tissue presence or injury and is not used to titrate levothyroxine.

66.B: Mild TSH elevation with normal FT4 is not severe hypothyroidism and is often a consequence rather than a cause of obesity.
66.C: Hypothyroidism is a rare cause of obesity; most childhood obesity is exogenous with preserved or accelerated linear growth.
66.D: Thyroidectomy has no role in mild hyperthyrotropinaemia with normal FT4.

67.A: Warm moist skin is a thyrotoxic sign; hypothyroidism causes cool, dry, rough skin.
67.C: Hyperreflexia with tremor reflects thyroid hormone excess, not hypothyroidism.
67.D: Persistent tachycardia suggests thyrotoxicosis; longstanding hypothyroidism causes bradycardia.

68.A: Urine osmolality assesses water balance and diabetes insipidus, not skeletal maturation.
68.B: Random blood glucose screens for hypoglycaemia or diabetes and cannot estimate bone age.
68.D: Serum sodium is an electrolyte measure with no bearing on skeletal maturity.

69.A: Normal velocity with short parents is the defining pattern of familial short stature, not a red flag.
69.B: A normal examination is reassuring and favours a normal variant rather than pathology.
69.C: A stable centile over years indicates normal growth velocity, typical of familial short stature.

70.B: Headaches and visual-field symptoms are not features of familial short stature and mandate neuro-imaging.
70.C: Neurological red flags exclude a normal variant; craniopharyngioma or another sellar mass must be sought.
70.D: Primary thyroiditis can slow growth but does not explain headaches and visual-field defects, which point to a sellar lesion.

71.A: Treatment does not mandate precocious puberty; untreated severe hypothyroidism itself may rarely cause precocity (Van Wyk-Grumbach syndrome).
71.C: Replacement produces catch-up growth, not gigantism; overly rapid correction may even advance bone age and limit final height.
71.D: Growth velocity usually improves with adequate replacement, so claiming no change ever is incorrect.

72.A: Delaying assessment leaves untreated cortisol deficiency and hypoglycaemia, which can be fatal in childhood.
72.B: Genetic testing may define aetiology later but does nothing for the immediate risk of adrenal crisis.
72.D: GH is not urgent and is not given at high dose; glucocorticoid replacement must come first for safety.

73.A: FT4 directly measures thyroid function but does not establish autoimmune aetiology.
73.B: TSH defines thyroid functional status rather than indicating autoimmunity.
73.C: Paired TSH and FT4 are the tests that define thyroid function, the opposite of what the stem asks.

74.B: Thyroxine would add to thyroid hormone excess and worsen palpitations and tremor.
74.C: Growth hormone has no role in hyperthyroidism and would not control adrenergic symptoms.
74.D: Glucocorticoids are used only short term in thyroid storm or orbitopathy, never as sole long-term therapy for symptoms.

75.A: High FT4 with suppressed TSH reflects thyroid hormone excess and says nothing about GH status.
75.C: Undertreatment produces high TSH and low or low-normal FT4, the opposite of this profile.
75.D: Coeliac disease impairs levothyroxine absorption, causing under- rather than over-replacement, and needs serology to confirm.
